BLACK DUST

By: Anina Peens | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
It's city synonymous with coal, Richards bay houses the continents largest coal port terminal... but why has life here, become so unbearable lately?

Unique Selling Point:
Black dust everywhere... life in the coastal town of Richardsbay has become unbearable with residents living like prisoners, hiding from the dust clouds suffocating their lives.

Summary:
It’s the health of the people versus politics in Richards Bay.
Entire suburbs, houses, schools and hospitals are covered in black dust emanating from a massive influx of coal trucks into the bay. Illegal stockpiles are popping up like mushrooms, not adhering to any rules and regulations. Clouds of black dust fill the sky affecting the most vital element for survival, oxygen.
Health care providers receive record number of daily incidents of a variety of lung-based illnesses directly related to coal dust inhalation. A Local pharmacy says it receives 30 to 40 patients daily, referred by doctors. The number of incidents seems to have tripled over the last six month. Now that its winter, and there is less wind, the coal dust in the air is omnipresent.
Businesses are closing, others up and leave as the authorities, yet again, turn a blind eye.



Further information:
It’s the full circle; the effects of the coal mining conundrum in Mpumalanga, has become a question of life and death.
Over the last two years, we have frequently revisited coal mining and its effects in Mpumalanga;
- The illegal mines popping up around the province, the low-grade coal supplied to Eskom, causing breakages at the power stations, resulting in loadshedding.
- National infrastructure further compromised as suspected sabotage to railway systems causes the increase of trucks on the roads.
- Thousands of trucks cause fatal accidents, constant traffic collisions and gigantic potholes, putting more lives in danger.
-
We have reported on the railway problem and used Majuba power station as example to focus on the coal suppliers, connected to Eskom and referred to as the coal mafia. High ranking politicians are said to be connected to most of the coal mines through family members. We have also reported on fatal accidents caused by the coal trucks on the Richards Bay corridor via Pongola.

Black Lung Port takes the story further as operations, that seem to be unregulated by government, are now causing a massive health crisis in the bay city.

Since last year, the number of coal trucks moving into the port city of Richards Bay, have increased to unfathomable numbers.
The story is twofold:
1. Thousands of coal trucks dump loads of mostly second grade coal on illegal stockpiles popping up around the city. As soon as the municipality closes one stockpile, another opens somewhere else. Owners of the stockpiles are connected to the coal mines in Mpumalanga and are not to be held accountable to anyone. Dust from the stockpiles blow across the city, making life unbearable.
2. On the one side of the harbor, Richard’s Bay Coal Terminals brings in coal using trains. Dust emissions caused are minimal. But on the other side of the harbor, coal is dumped directly from trucks, causing even more dust clouds across the city in addition to the illegal stockpiles.

The municipality has reached out to national government for help, but without success. The municipality is a coalition between IP and DA and politics between the municipality and the national ANC may be at play. It is evident from dealings with a local resident Tashni Govender who seems to have connections high up in the ANC. She does as she pleases. She rents properties and sublets it to stockpiles owners. These properties are in residential suburbs and when the wind blows, it covers homes in black dust. The municipality was granted an interdict from the Durban high court, forcing her to remove the stockpiles, but she ignored it. Now she is in contempt of court. The Provincial legislate in Durban then phones the Richardsbay municipality asking them for leniency against Mrs Governdor. Who is she working for?


Further to the problem with opportunities like Govendor, there are no by-laws to regulate the enormous pollution caused and the municipality relies only on national environmental bylaws. Case specific by-laws for the crisis in Richard’s Bay have been drafted, and that’s about where it ends.
The municipality acquired an air pollution monitoring system but does not have the expertise to analyze the data.
Meanwhile, hospitals, clinics, pharmacies and health care centers are flood with new patients every day. And it is not basic nasal allergies caused by the dust anymore, it is severe respiratory illnesses that have in many cases become chronic.

- We have access to a complaints data base on which illnesses are reported, daily. We speak to people who have been hospitalized as a result of the coal dust.
- One man filmed his daughter playing in the garden every day, for over six months. Every time, she comes in from the garden, the layer of black dust on her skin, is thicker.
- People have been tracking the dust levels in swimming pools that clearly show the built-up.

Two nights stay
Two flights

BLACK DUST DRAFT SCRIPT: FINAL SCRIPT TO MIX

OPENING SEQUENCE: SCENE SETTER

6 “MUSIC AND MONTAGE OF COAL AND MINES

VO
A dirty fossil fuel… much in demand

PAUSE

VO
Transported from inland mines to a harbour on KZN’s north coast, coal’s grubby tracks run deep.

VO
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is starving countries of the vital fuels needed to meet their energy demands. It’s boomtime for global coal suppliers, like South Africa.

But it comes at a cost… paid for in the decimation of infrastructure by the endless trucks taking the coal to port…

…where the journey ends in a chaotic haze of exhaust fumes and black dust.

First Fade to Black (end of intro sequence)

VO
Welcome to Richards Bay… once a holiday and retirement destination, now reduced to a grimey wasteland.

SANET WESSELS: RESIDENT
“Die stof, die stof is verskriklik”
SUB: The dust, the dust is terrible”

NARDUS JOOSTE: BUSINESS OWNER
Pick one of this ceiling boards for me.
MAC: Is this what it… hold on…
MAC BLOWS IT:
Mac: I actually thought the back of this panel was black

VO
This is a story about how a town is being sacrificed for greed and opportunism.

Africa Holdings unknown old indian man
MAC: But do you know that the court said this is illegal now? Are you guys still operating here?”
OLD MAN: You can see the operation
MAC: It’s busy! It's busy here!

ACT 1

NARDUS JOOSTE: BUSINESS OWNER (driving)
I’m 15 years now in Richards Bay and when I moved to Richards Bay, it was the cleanest, everything was maintained. I told my wife, listen, this is where I wanna stay. But you can look at our roads, you can look at the dust, everything here.

VO
An estimated 50 thousand trucks come to Richards Bay each month. Business owners like Nardus Jooste have had enough.

NARDUS JOOSTE: BUSINESS OWNER (driving)
All the businesses are suffering about this…I mean you can’t get entrance to your shop, your customers can’t get entrance to your shop.

VO
And with the trucks gridlocked amid crumbling infrastructure, coal dust is swept across the town - an inescapable, dirty plume.

NARDUS JOOSTE: BUSINESS OWNER (get out car, side of road)
I just want to show you the condition that the whole Richards Bay. If you look at this dust here, I mean, its black.
MAC: everywhere, this is everywhere now
NARDUS: Everywhere, we can stop a few places and you can look inside it, there is metal pieces.
MAC: Has it always been like this?
NARDUS: No, never. Richards Bay was never in this condition.

VO
The slightest wind causes dust storms, covering entire suburbs.

SANET WESSELS: RESIDENT
“Ons huise is permanent swart, met swart stof”
SUB: Our houses are permanently covered in black dust”

VO
Sanet Wessels has been living here for more than 30 years.

SANET WESSELS: RESIDENT
“Ons vensters is permanent toe”
SUBS: “Our windows are permanently closed”.
“Ons het nou ‘n kroniese sinus probleem, die kinders hoes erg en veral as die wind bietjie waai…”
SUBS: We have a chronic sinus problem, the kids are always coughing, especially if the wind blows.

LINK (inspecting leaves)
Everything here gets covered in this black dust, the trees, the grass, the plants. I mean look at this, it doesn’t even move. Now if it sits like this on a leaf, imagine what it does to your lungs.

Possible 17” cut
VO
In Richards Bay, venturing outdoors has become a health risk.

SANET WESSELS: RESIDENT
Ons voel half of ons ingehok word nou, ons gaan nie meer so gereeld buite toe wat ons gaan stap nie. Ons is baie lief om te gaan stap. Ons stap gladnie meer nie want, as ons terugkom, ‘n uur of twee daarna dan het ons hoofpyn…ons oë brand of die kind begin hoes”
SUBS: We feel caged in. We don’t go outside anymore to go for walks. We love going for walks, but we don’t anymore because when we return, the headaches come, an hour or so later. Our eyes burn, the children cough”

VO
Residents have little hope of their town one day returning to normal; not when so many vested interests, including the mines, transport companies and even the State are cashing in.

NARDUS JOOSTE: BUSINESS OWNER (intersection outside shop)
It’s like a desert storm that goes over this place, and it doesn’t help if you complain, to who? Nothing ever happens. I think the story is much deeper than what we realise”.

ACT 2

VO
And yet, there’s a prime example of how things SHOULD be done, in plain sight. You see, Richard’s Bay Port is home to TWO coal operations. One is state run, the other is privately-owned. No guessing which of the two is more efficient.

The Richards Bay Coal Terminal, a handling facility for coal exporters, is run from this building. It ships mind boggling volumes of coal to the global market in a system reliant on 70 kilometres of conveyor belts.

LINK (in front of massive ship)
So, to put all of this into perspective, this ship alone will probably carry up to a 157 thousand tons of coal and when it is at full capacity, all of that red, about 19 metres, will be below the water.

VO
The privately owned terminal loads a ship a day and, crucially, it relies on coal delivered by train – meaning, very little dust! But there’s a significant variable in the mix: TFR, or Transnet Freight Rail.

Alan Waller
We are highly dependent on government in terms of TFR and the ability to deliver. When it works well, it works really well.

VO
But the opposite is also true. Alan Waller, the terminal’s CEO, says there’s currently a shortage of about 160 trains in the coal system.

ALAN CEO
MAC: Why don’t you use trucks here?
ALAN: To put road trucks into the terminal would be problematic just logistically. We are 8-9 kilometres into the port on a single road. If you look at what’s happened on the roads just in terms of the volume that is already moving on road, it would be extremely irresponsible of us to also consider going to road.

VO
Bu that doesn’t seem a consideration on the other side of the port; where noxious, noisy chaos awaits us.

ACT 3

VO
It’s a slow, dirty drive into side of the port managed by parastatal, Transnet. Around us, trains stand idle but there’s no shortage of trucks waiting to get in.

Just one train could replace between 200 and 400 trucks. It’s the port authority’s job to maintain and improve infrastructure but there’s little sign of that happening here.

Most of the 90 kilometres of conveyor belts are unused. A significant section, apparently lost to arson in 2021, is yet to be repaired.

PAUSE

This part of the port, unlike its efficient, privately-run neighbour, now relies on an endless line of trucks stretching from here towards Pongola 200km away.

DRIVER: Hey bra, sometimes we wait maybe three days outside, before getting in”
MAC: And when you get in what happens?
Driver: Eish, I don’t know what’s the problem here
MAC: Where do you offload?
Driver: By the harbour there are different places there, it is not one place, it is different places……

Note: After the UPS of the truck pulling off, lets go straight to VO to quicken the pace.

Those “different places” are a series of uncovered stockpiles, adding to the massive dust problem.

PAUSE

VO
But what’s more is that the stockpiles are not limited to the Transnet operation.
They are popping up outside the port, and most, are illegal.

LINK
So, the idea here with these stockpiles, because of the congestion on the N2, what these drivers do is, come here, drop off the coal here, and then go back to the coal mines and then other trucks, they come and pick it up and take it to the coal terminal. That then makes the delivery times much shorter, and they don’t have to waste so much time on the road, because if you are not delivering, you are not making money.

VO
Rogue landlords rent space to transport companies for big money. It’s another headache in a long list for the municipal manager, Nkosenye Zulu.

ZULU, MUNICIPALITY
These are companies that entered into deals with owners of open sites, because there is a lot of money to be made in this”.

VO
Zulu shows us at least half a dozen court orders demanding the closure of illegal stockpiles, but sometimes, not even that is enough to stop them.

ZULU: Group Africa is completely ignoring the orders of the court.

VO
This yard, operated by Group Africa Holdings, was ordered to close by the courts. Its sole owner is 21-year old, Varenya Govender, but it’s alleged the brains behind the business is her mother, Tashanie. The company sublets space to transport companies for hundreds of thousands of Rand a month.

MAC: Do you know where we can get a hold of her?
Man: In Durban
Mac: In Durban… She doesnt come here?
Man: they come once a month
Mac: but do you know that the court said this is illegal, the courts have interdicted her and said that she must stop doing this? Did you know that?
Man: No we’re not aware of that.
Mac: You’re not aware…

VO
Living in Durban, mother and daughter are spared the impact of uncovered coal on this once prosperous town. We call Tashanie for answers, and she initially agrees to an interview.

MAC: There is a court order that there shouldn’t be any stockpiling happening on this land and it looks like it is still business as usual?
TASHANIE: The matter is on appeal, the interim order which has been served is being appealed and the matter is in court, so nothing has been decided as yet.

VO
Tashani later decides against the interview, but her lawyers respond to our questions saying the court order is being contested and telling us to stop contacting their client. In a sinister twist Zulu tells us the move to shut them down was an unpopular one.

MUNICIPAL MANAGER, UMHLATHUZE MUNICIPALITY
Instead of this company complying with a court order that was issued by a sitting judge, we started receiving calls from politicians, from very very serious individuals whose names I will not mention, trying to intercede on behalf of this company.
MAC: No, it’s corruption. Why are the politicians getting involved, it's not their land?
ZULU: Exactly,

CLOSING

VO
As the dust and decay spread, more and more people are leaving Richard’s Bay. For Nardus, though, that’s not an option.

NARDUS JOOSTE: BUSINESS OWNER
This is my life, this is my pension. I am not young anymore, so I can’t pack up, where will I go?



DURATION - 12:30

VO

VO
Richards Bay has always been Africa’s largest coal exporter. But why are residents rapidly getting sick?

NARDUS JOOSTE: BUSINESS OWNER
Richards Bay was never in this condition.

PROMO 3

VO
Thousands of trucks pile up on the N2 to Richards Bay… causing havoc.

MUNICIPAL MANAGER, UMHLATHUZE MUNICIPALITY
Some motorists have lost their lives because of these trucks…

VO
And where their journey ends, life for residents is unbearable.

NARDUS JOOSTE: BUSINESS OWNER
Look at our roads, you can look at the dust.

VO
We set off to the country’s largest coal port.

SANET WESSELS: RESIDENT Ons voel half of ons ingehok word nou, ons gaan nie meer so gereeld buite toe wat ons gaan stap nie. Ons is baie lief om te gaan stap. Ons stap gladnie meer nie want, as ons terugkom, ‘n uur of twee daarna dan het ons hoofpyn…ons oë brand of die kind begin hoes” SUBS: We feel caged in. We don’t go outside anymore to go for walks. We love going for walks, but we don’t anymore because when we return, the headaches come, an hour or so later. Our eyes burn, the children cough” VO Residents have little hope of their town one day returning to normal; not when so many vested interests, including the mines, transport companies and even the State are cashing in. NARDUS JOOSTE: BUSINESS OWNER (intersection outside shop) It’s like a desert storm that goes over this place, and it doesn’t help if you complain, to who? Nothing ever happens. I think the story is much deeper than what we realise”. ACT 2 VO And yet, there’s a prime example of how things SHOULD be done, in plain sight. You see, Richard’s Bay Port is home to TWO coal operations. One is state run, the other is privately-owned. No guessing which of the two is more efficient. The Richards Bay Coal Terminal, a handling facility for coal exporters, is run from this building. It ships mind boggling volumes of coal to the global market in a system reliant on 70 kilometres of conveyor belts. LINK (in front of massive ship) So, to put all of this into perspective, this ship alone will probably carry up to a 157 thousand tons of coal and when it is at full capacity, all of that red, about 19 metres, will be below the water. VO The privately owned terminal loads a ship a day and, crucially, it relies on coal delivered by train – meaning, very little dust! But there’s a significant variable in the mix: TFR, or Transnet Freight Rail. Alan Waller We are highly dependent on government in terms of TFR and the ability to deliver. When it works well, it works really well. VO But the opposite is also true. Alan Waller, the terminal’s CEO, says there’s currently a shortage of about 160 trains in the coal system. ALAN CEO MAC: Why don’t you use trucks here? ALAN: To put road trucks into the terminal would be problematic just logistically. We are 8-9 kilometres into the port on a single road. If you look at what’s happened on the roads just in terms of the volume that is already moving on road, it would be extremely irresponsible of us to also consider going to road. VO Bu that doesn’t seem a consideration on the other side of the port; where noxious, noisy chaos awaits us. ACT 3 VO It’s a slow, dirty drive into side of the port managed by parastatal, Transnet. Around us, trains stand idle but there’s no shortage of trucks waiting to get in. Just one train could replace between 200 and 400 trucks. It’s the port authority’s job to maintain and improve infrastructure but there’s little sign of that happening here. Most of the 90 kilometres of conveyor belts are unused. A significant section, apparently lost to arson in 2021, is yet to be repaired. PAUSE This part of the port, unlike its efficient, privately-run neighbour, now relies on an endless line of trucks stretching from here towards Pongola 200km away. DRIVER: Hey bra, sometimes we wait maybe three days outside, before getting in” MAC: And when you get in what happens? Driver: Eish, I don’t know what’s the problem here MAC: Where do you offload? Driver: By the harbour there are different places there, it is not one place, it is different places…… Note: After the UPS of the truck pulling off, lets go straight to VO to quicken the pace. Those “different places” are a series of uncovered stockpiles, adding to the massive dust problem. PAUSE VO But what’s more is that the stockpiles are not limited to the Transnet operation. They are popping up outside the port, and most, are illegal. LINK So, the idea here with these stockpiles, because of the congestion on the N2, what these drivers do is, come here, drop off the coal here, and then go back to the coal mines and then other trucks, they come and pick it up and take it to the coal terminal. That then makes the delivery times much shorter, and they don’t have to waste so much time on the road, because if you are not delivering, you are not making money. VO Rogue landlords rent space to transport companies for big money. It’s another headache in a long list for the municipal manager, Nkosenye Zulu. ZULU, MUNICIPALITY These are companies that entered into deals with owners of open sites, because there is a lot of money to be made in this”. VO Zulu shows us at least half a dozen court orders demanding the closure of illegal stockpiles, but sometimes, not even that is enough to stop them. ZULU: Group Africa is completely ignoring the orders of the court. VO This yard, operated by Group Africa Holdings, was ordered to close by the courts. Its sole owner is 21-year old, Varenya Govender, but it’s alleged the brains behind the business is her mother, Tashanie. The company sublets space to transport companies for hundreds of thousands of Rand a month. MAC: Do you know where we can get a hold of her? Man: In Durban Mac: In Durban… She doesnt come here? Man: they come once a month Mac: but do you know that the court said this is illegal, the courts have interdicted her and said that she must stop doing this? Did you know that? Man: No we’re not aware of that. Mac: You’re not aware… VO Living in Durban, mother and daughter are spared the impact of uncovered coal on this once prosperous town. We call Tashanie for answers, and she initially agrees to an interview. MAC: There is a court order that there shouldn’t be any stockpiling happening on this land and it looks like it is still business as usual? TASHANIE: The matter is on appeal, the interim order which has been served is being appealed and the matter is in court, so nothing has been decided as yet. VO Tashani later decides against the interview, but her lawyers respond to our questions saying the court order is being contested and telling us to stop contacting their client. In a sinister twist Zulu tells us the move to shut them down was an unpopular one. MUNICIPAL MANAGER, UMHLATHUZE MUNICIPALITY Instead of this company complying with a court order that was issued by a sitting judge, we started receiving calls from politicians, from very very serious individuals whose names I will not mention, trying to intercede on behalf of this company. MAC: No, it’s corruption. Why are the politicians getting involved, it's not their land? ZULU: Exactly, CLOSING VO As the dust and decay spread, more and more people are leaving Richard’s Bay. For Nardus, though, that’s not an option. NARDUS JOOSTE: BUSINESS OWNER This is my life, this is my pension. I am not young anymore, so I can’t pack up, where will I go? DURATION - 12:30 TIMELINE PROMOS PROMO 1 VO Richards Bay is covered in black dust. SANET WESSELS: RESIDENT Ons huise is permanent swart, met swart stof VO Doors and windows are shut and children don't play outside. NARDUS JOOSTE: BUSINESS OWNER If the wind blows, it's like a desert storm that goes over this place. VO We visit Africa’s largest coal port. PROMO 2 VO Many have packed up and left. They couldn't stand it anymore. SANET WESSELS: RESIDENT Die stof, die stof is verskriklik, dit begin nou ons gesondheid affekteer VO Richards Bay has always been Africa’s largest coal exporter. But why are residents rapidly getting sick? NARDUS JOOSTE: BUSINESS OWNER Richards Bay was never in this condition. PROMO 3 VO Thousands of trucks pile up on the N2 to Richards Bay… causing havoc. MUNICIPAL MANAGER, UMHLATHUZE MUNICIPALITY Some motorists have lost their lives because of these trucks… VO And where their journey ends, life for residents is unbearable. NARDUS JOOSTE: BUSINESS OWNER Look at our roads, you can look at the dust. VO We set off to the country’s largest coal port. ALT SANET WESSELS: RESIDENT SOURCE: CARD 3 CLIP 00005 20:28:57:10 “Ons is vir 31 jaar in Richardsbaai en… 20:29:36:08 “Hierdie afgelope, ek sal sê seker so 18 maande, het dit erg begin te raak maar dit is nou op hierdie stadium baie erg”.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): It's city synonymous with coal, Richards bay houses the continents largest coal port terminal... but why has life here, become so unbearable lately?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Black dust everywhere... life in the coastal town of Richardsbay has become unbearable with residents living like prisoners, hiding from the dust clouds suffocating their lives.
metadata.Summary: It’s the health of the people versus politics in Richards Bay. Entire suburbs, houses, schools and hospitals are covered in black dust emanating from a massive influx of coal trucks into the bay. Illegal stockpiles are popping up like mushrooms, not adhering to any rules and regulations. Clouds of black dust fill the sky affecting the most vital element for survival, oxygen. Health care providers receive record number of daily incidents of a variety of lung-based illnesses directly related to coal dust inhalation. A Local pharmacy says it receives 30 to 40 patients daily, referred by doctors. The number of incidents seems to have tripled over the last six month. Now that its winter, and there is less wind, the coal dust in the air is omnipresent. Businesses are closing, others up and leave as the authorities, yet again, turn a blind eye.
metadata.Further information: It’s the full circle; the effects of the coal mining conundrum in Mpumalanga, has become a question of life and death. Over the last two years, we have frequently revisited coal mining and its effects in Mpumalanga; - The illegal mines popping up around the province, the low-grade coal supplied to Eskom, causing breakages at the power stations, resulting in loadshedding. - National infrastructure further compromised as suspected sabotage to railway systems causes the increase of trucks on the roads. - Thousands of trucks cause fatal accidents, constant traffic collisions and gigantic potholes, putting more lives in danger. - We have reported on the railway problem and used Majuba power station as example to focus on the coal suppliers, connected to Eskom and referred to as the coal mafia. High ranking politicians are said to be connected to most of the coal mines through family members. We have also reported on fatal accidents caused by the coal trucks on the Richards Bay corridor via Pongola. Black Lung Port takes the story further as operations, that seem to be unregulated by government, are now causing a massive health crisis in the bay city. Since last year, the number of coal trucks moving into the port city of Richards Bay, have increased to unfathomable numbers. The story is twofold: 1. Thousands of coal trucks dump loads of mostly second grade coal on illegal stockpiles popping up around the city. As soon as the municipality closes one stockpile, another opens somewhere else. Owners of the stockpiles are connected to the coal mines in Mpumalanga and are not to be held accountable to anyone. Dust from the stockpiles blow across the city, making life unbearable. 2. On the one side of the harbor, Richard’s Bay Coal Terminals brings in coal using trains. Dust emissions caused are minimal. But on the other side of the harbor, coal is dumped directly from trucks, causing even more dust clouds across the city in addition to the illegal stockpiles. The municipality has reached out to national government for help, but without success. The municipality is a coalition between IP and DA and politics between the municipality and the national ANC may be at play. It is evident from dealings with a local resident Tashni Govender who seems to have connections high up in the ANC. She does as she pleases. She rents properties and sublets it to stockpiles owners. These properties are in residential suburbs and when the wind blows, it covers homes in black dust. The municipality was granted an interdict from the Durban high court, forcing her to remove the stockpiles, but she ignored it. Now she is in contempt of court. The Provincial legislate in Durban then phones the Richardsbay municipality asking them for leniency against Mrs Governdor. Who is she working for? Further to the problem with opportunities like Govendor, there are no by-laws to regulate the enormous pollution caused and the municipality relies only on national environmental bylaws. Case specific by-laws for the crisis in Richard’s Bay have been drafted, and that’s about where it ends. The municipality acquired an air pollution monitoring system but does not have the expertise to analyze the data. Meanwhile, hospitals, clinics, pharmacies and health care centers are flood with new patients every day. And it is not basic nasal allergies caused by the dust anymore, it is severe respiratory illnesses that have in many cases become chronic. - We have access to a complaints data base on which illnesses are reported, daily. We speak to people who have been hospitalized as a result of the coal dust. - One man filmed his daughter playing in the garden every day, for over six months. Every time, she comes in from the garden, the layer of black dust on her skin, is thicker. - People have been tracking the dust levels in swimming pools that clearly show the built-up.
